body_markdown: Nutanix Prism Central supports extensive use of category-based entity assignments, helping the configuration of what can often be complex rules. A practical, real-world example of these complex rules is VM-to-VM firewalling – the ability to prevent “this VM” from talking to “that VM”. Throughout this article, this will be referred to as microsegmentation and will be managed with Nutanix Flow Network Security policies. For example, a classic 3-tier web application could contain components such as web servers running Apache or Nginx, backend database servers running MySQL or MariaDB and frontend proxy or load-balancing servers running HAProxy. In this article, we’ll explore how DevOps and scripting teams can easily automate VM category assignments, helping organisations control and restrict communication between application components based on defined policies. ## Requirements The web application in question is made up of 3 tiers. In the context of this specific demo, the *specific* software running in each tier isn’t relevant but has been labelled for simplicity. - Frontend proxy/load-balancing servers - Web servers - Database servers A typical traffic flow may be as follows: 1. User makes a request to the public IP address. This request is handled by the public-facing or publicly-accessible proxy/load-balancer. 2. The proxy/load-balancer selects a web server from the available pool, depending on which server has the most available capacity. 3. The web server’s application logic makes appropriate requests to the database servers, depending on persistent data required by the app. In this configuration, there is no architectural reason for the proxy/load-balancer to directly contact the database server, since those requests are only necessary from the web servers. Without any component isolation in place, it is possible for the proxy/load-balancer to contact the database server, creating a potential attack vector for unwanted requests. This unwanted attack vector is highlighted in red below. Unwanted communication direct from the proxy/load-balancer servers to database servers ## Configuration This article focuses on the configuration of VM category assignments; creation of Nutanix Flow Network Security policies is beyond the scope of this article and is documented in the[Nutanix Flow Network Security Next-Gen documentation](https://portal.nutanix.com/page/documents/list?type=software&filterKey=software&filterVal=Flow%20Network%20Security%20Next-Gen) . However, for the purposes of this demo, no network security policy is required. From a category perspective, our demo environment has 2 categories. Prism Central categories are configured within the Admin Center: Admin Center > Categories For this demo, our categories are configured as follows: Two category keys, each containing a single value Along with these categories, the demo will use a single virtual machine for category assignments. The demo’s VM is named` cr-ubuntu-lcm-download-server` . ### Script Specifications Accompanying the complete demo script that will be discussed in upcoming steps, 2 JSON files are used to specify the name of the VM(s) that will have categories assigned and the categories that will be assigned to them. The JSON spec file contents match the VM name and category names outlined above. #### VM spec ```text [ { "name": "cr-ubuntu-lcm-download-server" } ] ``` #### Category spec ```text [ { "key": "category_key1", "value": "category_value1", "description": "Test category 1" }, { "key": "category_key2", "value": "category_value2", "description": "Test category 2" } ] ``` ## Demo Setup If you are following this demo in your own environment, the following steps must be followed. 1. Clone the entire NutanixDev Code Samples repository. This ensures the` tme` support library is available with the demo script. 2. Create Prism Central entities to be used in the demo: - At least 1 category key with at least 1 category value. - At least 1 VM. 3. Edit the VM and category spec files to include VM names and category names matching values valid in your environment. - VM and category` extId` values are NOT required during setup; the script will extract those values during execution. **Note** : The demo script will prompt for confirmation at each step, but will result in live changes being made in your environment. This demo is not intended for use in a production environment. ## The Script The Python SDK demo script workflow is as follows. Important note: If your workflow prefers to implement Nutanix v4 REST APIs instead of the official SDKs, an accompanying` assign_categories_to_vms_client.py` has also been provided. 1. Collects information the user - Prism Central IP address or FQDN - Prism Central username - Prism Central password (not shown on screen) 2. Creates instances of the` VmmConfiguration` ,` VmmClient` and` PrismClient` classes. Note: the classes are imported and aliased: ```text from ntnx_vmm_py_client import Configuration as VMMConfiguration from ntnx_vmm_py_client import ApiClient as VMMClient from ntnx_prism_py_client import Configuration as PrismConfiguration from ntnx_prism_py_client import ApiClient as PrismClient # create the API class instances vmm_instance = ntnx_vmm_py_client.api.VmApi(api_client=vmm_client) prism_instance = ntnx_prism_py_client.api.CategoriesApi(api_client=prism_client) ``` 1. Loads the contents of the VM and category spec files. Both actions use a functions named` load_json_file` . ```text categories_data = load_json_file("assign_categories_to_vms_catspec.json") vms_data = load_json_file("assign_categories_to_vms_vmspec.json") ``` 1. To ensure no expected changes are made, the script then asks for confirmation before continuing. ```text confirm_assign = utils.confirm( "Assign categories to VMs? " "This will make category changes in your environment." ) if confirm_assign: ``` 1. The script then iterates over each VM in the spec file, carrying out some verification as it does so. 2. Then, for each VM, the script uses a function named` get_vm_ext_id` to get the VM’s unique ID, then requests the VM’s configuration and etag. ```text try: for vm_entry in vms_data: vm_name = vm_entry.get("name") or vm_entry.get("ext_id") ... vm_ext_id = get_vm_ext_id(vmm_instance, vm_name) ... # retrieve the VM to get its Etag print(f"Retrieving VM details for {vm_name} ...") existing_vm = vmm_instance.get_vm_by_id(vm_ext_id) existing_vm_etag = vmm_client.get_etag(existing_vm) ``` 1. When updating an entity using the Nutanix v4 APIs and SDKs, the request must be accompanied with the VM’s current etag. This prevents mid-air collisions during updates. ```text # add the Etag as If-Match header vmm_client.add_default_header( header_name="If-Match", header_value=existing_vm_etag ) ``` 1. The script then iterates over each category listed in the JSON spec file, checking for existence and, if the category is found, getting each category’s unique ID. ```text for category in categories_data: category_key = category.get("key") or category.get("name") category_value = category.get("value") ... # get the ext_id of the category from Prism Central category_ext_id = get_category_ext_id( prism_instance, category_key, category_value ) ``` 1. After building a list of the categories that will be assigned, the script can move onto the final step: category assignment. ```text # create the AssociateVmCategoriesParams object associate_params = ( AhvVmConfig.AssociateVmCategoriesParams.AssociateVmCategoriesParams( # noqa #pylint: disable=line-too-long, redefined-builtin categories=category_refs ) ) # associate the categories with the VM vmm_instance.associate_categories( vm_ext_id, associate_params, async_req=False ) ``` Throughout the process, the script provides meaningful information regarding entity request status and subsequent update actions. ## Testing the script Now that the important parts of the script have been outlined in detail, let’s look at what a complete test run looks like. ### Virtual Environment The NutanixDev code sample repository uses` uv` for Python package management and is distributed with a project-specific` pyproject.toml` . This file can be found in the same directory as the demo script. 1. Install dependencies ```text # install and synchronise Python dependencies uv sync ``` ### Run the script 1. Run the script, replacing` ` and` ` with values matching your environment. ```text uv run assign_categories_to_vms_sdk.py --pc_ip --username ``` ### Script output The following screenshot demonstrates the workflow outlined above. Note the script prompting for the user’s password, prompting for confirmation to continue, then showing category` extId` details as each category is assigned to the VM. Demonstrating script output and successful VM category assignment As can be seen above, the virtual machine` cr-ubuntu-lcm-download-server` has had the following categories assigned: - ` category_key1:category_value1` - ` category_key2:category_value2` ## Why do this? Security and compliance could be considered two of the most important reasons to isolate services from each other in a production environment. Whilst every environment will likely maintain its own official posture on how best to meet security and compliance requirements, applying least-privilege access to application services is a commonly adopted security practice, subject to an organisation’s specific requirements and risk profile. ## An Additional Use Case Throughout this article, we’ve discussed and demonstrated how to use the Nutanix v4 Python SDK and REST APIs to assign multiple categories to multiple VMs. The provided JSON specs can be easily extended to include a list of VMs instead a single VM, and the JSON spec can be easily extended to include a larger list of categories, if required. However, user-initiated configurations like this are just one of the ways the Nutanix v4 APIs can be used. ### What about AI? With AI becoming an increasingly common approach to code generation, report creation and information gathering, it makes sense for the Nutanix v4 APIs to exist they way they do and be accessed the way they are. Let’s look at a quick, conceptual example. A systems administrator, Taylor, uses approved AI tools to complete various daily tasks. Today’s task is to complete the same steps as the demo script: assign multiple categories to multiple VMs. Since APIs are, by definition, a way of accessing services through well recognised protocols and methods, AI systems can be configured to interact with Nutanix v4 APIs, although implementation effort will depend on the tools, workflows, and environment involved. Whilst specific agentic AI systems and their capabilities are beyond the scope of this article, Taylor could provide instructions that may enable an approved AI system to assist with automating portions of these tasks. > Build a script that accepts a list of virtual machines and Prism Central categories from an on-disk JSON file. Using the virtual machine and category names from the JSON files, iterate over each virtual machine, get the virtual machine details, then assign each category to that virtual machine. As the task proceeds, keep a list and count of both successful and failed category assignments, providing a report to the user at the conclusion of the script. The Nutanix v4 API and model definitions are available at https://developers.nutanix.com. This basic prompt demonstrates a starting point for using an agentic AI system to complete what could become a common task. ## The Results When applied to Nutanix Flow Network Security policies, the results of carrying out this task can be visualized as shown below. This is exact same application architecture shown earlier in this article, but without the unexpected communication between proxy/load-balancer and database servers. No unwanted communication direct between proxy/load-balancer and database servers ### An actual example When we apply this approach to a real Nutanix Flow Network Security policy and attempt communication between the isolated servers, the example demonstrates category-based traffic being blocked under the configured policy. Example of network communications between isolated VMs being blocked by Nutanix Flow Network Security Policy; both VMs are assigned to Prism Central categories belonging to the security policy ## Downloadable Code Sample To view, download and use the[code sample accompanying this article](https://github.com/nutanixdev/code-samples/blob/master/python/v4api_sdk/assign_categories_to_vms_requests.py) , see the NutanixDev Code Samples GitHub repository. [Important](https://github.com/nutanixdev/code-samples/tree/master/python/v4api_sdk/tme) : Make sure to clone to the entire repository when using the code sample. This helps ensure the imported` tme` module is available when running the script. ## Conclusion This article demonstrates how easily the Nutanix v4 APIs and SDKs can be used to assign virtual machines to Prism Central categories. In this demo, the categories have been used by Nutanix Flow Network Security policies and specifically block communication between the demo application’s proxy/load-balancer and database servers. ## Related Information - [Nutanix API User Guide](https://www.nutanix.dev/nutanix-api-user-guide/) - [Nutanix v4 API documentation](https://developers.nutanix.com/)
